Le Colorado a creusé le Grand Canyon en des millions d’années.
A state in the western United States, the 38th state. Capital and largest city: Denver.
We went skiing in Colorado last winter.
Nous sommes allés skier au Colorado l’hiver dernier.
(uncountable) The spectral composition of visible light.
Humans and birds can perceive color.
Les humains et les oiseaux perçoivent la couleur.
Human skin tone, especially as an indicator of race or ethnicity.
Color has been a sensitive issue in many societies.
La couleur de peau a été une question sensible dans de nombreuses sociétés.
A particular set of visible spectral compositions, perceived or named as a class.
What color are your bf's eyes?
De quelle couleur sont les yeux de ton copain ?
Conveying color, as opposed to shades of gray.
Color television and movies were considered a great improvement over black and white.
La télévision et le cinéma en couleur furent considérés comme un grand progrès par rapport au noir et blanc.
We could color the walls red.
On pourrait peindre les murs en rouge.
(intransitive) To apply colors to the areas within the boundaries of a line drawing using colored markers or crayons.
Mon enfant de maternelle adore colorier.
(of a person or their face) To become red through increased blood flow.
Her face colored as she realized her mistake.
Son visage rougit quand elle comprit son erreur.
That interpretation certainly colors my perception of the book.
Cette interprétation colore certainement ma perception du livre.
To attribute a quality to; to portray (as).
They tried to colour the industrial unrest as a merely local matter.
Ils ont tenté de faire passer l’agitation sociale pour une affaire purement locale.
(of a, person or animal) Unable to distinguish between two or more primary colors (usually red and green).
Holding no prejudice based on skin color or race; not paying attention to skin color.
Because mass incarceration is officially colorblind, it seems inconceivable that the system could function much like a racial caste system.
2012, Michelle Alexander, The New Jim Crow, →ISBN, page 183
Comme l’incarcération de masse est officiellement aveugle à la couleur, il semble inconcevable que le système puisse fonctionner comme un système de castes raciales.
Having a particular color or kind of color.
The room was red, with a dark-colored rug.
La pièce était rouge, avec un tapis aux tons sombres.
The singer wore a colored shirt.
Le chanteur portait une chemise colorée.
Biased; pervasively (but potentially subtly) influenced in a particular way.
The organization's traditions and culture are inwardly focused. It is not conceivable that an alternative solution could exist. This results in a very colored view of the marketplace.
2001, Bernard H. Boar, The Art of Strategic Planning for Information…
Les traditions et la culture de l’organisation sont tournées vers l’intérieur. Il est inconcevable qu’une autre solution puisse exister. Il en résulte une vision très partiale du marché.

Belonging to a multiracial ethnic group or category, having ancestry from more than one of the racial groups of Southern Africa (black, white, and Asian). (Under apartheid, used as a metadescription for mixed-race people and peoples such as the Cape Coloureds.)
Most of the colored community speaks Afrikaans, whereas languages like Xhosa or Venda are typically spoken by blacks and English is spoken mostly by whites.
La majeure partie de la communauté métisse (« coloured ») parle l’afrikaans, tandis que le xhosa ou le venda sont généralement parlés par les Noirs, et l’anglais surtout par les Blancs.
Wash colored items separately from whites and darks to prevent the colors from bleeding.
Lavez les articles de couleur séparément des blancs et des foncés, pour éviter que les couleurs ne déteignent.
Of skin color other than white; in particular, black.
(South Africa) A person having ancestry from more than one of the racial groups of Southern Africa (black, white, and Asian); a colored person.
un étalage de fleurs haut en couleur
He had a colourful career in the music industry.
Il a eu une carrière mouvementée dans l’industrie musicale.
Profane, obscene, offensive (usually in the phrase colourful language).
Hussain celebrated reaching his ton with a gesture towards the media centre, pointing to the number three on the back of his shirt and offering some colourful language.
2002 July 14, “Did Hussain go too far?”, in BBC Sport, archived from…
Hussain a célébré son siècle par un geste vers le centre de presse, montrant le numéro trois au dos de son maillot et lâchant quelques mots fleuris.
A youthful or inexperienced person; a novice.
He is still a colt in politics.
Il est encore un bleu en politique.
A professional cricketer during his first season.
The young colts impressed the selectors in the practice match.
Les jeunes de l’équipe ont impressionné les sélectionneurs lors du match d’entraînement.
A person who makes a great discovery.
(architecture) A solid upright structure designed usually to support a larger structure above it, such as a roof or horizontal beam, but sometimes…
A body of text meant to be read line by line, especially in printed material that has multiple adjacent such on a single page.
It was too hard to read the text across the whole page, so I split it into two columns.
C’était trop difficile de lire le texte sur toute la largeur de la page, alors je l’ai réparti en deux colonnes.
A unit of width, especially of advertisements, in a periodical, equivalent to the width of a usual column of text.
Each column inch costs $300 a week; this ad is four columns by three inches, so will run $3600 a week.
Chaque pouce-colonne coûte 300 dollars par semaine ; cette annonce fait quatre colonnes sur trois pouces, elle reviendra donc à 3 600 dollars par semaine.
(chemistry) An instrument used to separate the different components of a liquid or to purify chemical compounds.
The mixture was purified on a silica column.
Le mélange a été purifié sur une colonne de silice.
A recurring feature in a periodical, especially an opinion piece, especially by a single author or small rotating group of authors, or on a single theme.
His initial foray into print media was as the author of a weekly column in his elementary-school newspaper.
Ses débuts dans la presse écrite furent comme auteur d’une chronique hebdomadaire dans le journal de son école primaire.
A regular writer of a column, such as in a magazine or newspaper.
A state of unconsciousness from which one may not wake up, usually induced by some form of trauma.
(astronomy) A cloud of dust surrounding the nucleus of a comet.
A toothed implement for grooming the hair or (formerly) for keeping it in place.
A fleshy growth on the top of the head of some birds and reptiles; crest.

2001, Julian Sprung, Invertebrates: A Quick Reference Guide, page 35
Les cténophores sont des créatures planctoniques, de la taille et de la forme d’un kiwi ou d’un raisin, portant des rangées de « peignes » battants.
(transitive, especially of hair or fur) To groom with a toothed implement, especially a comb.
(transitive) To separate choice cotton fibers from worsted cloth fibers.
(transitive) To search thoroughly as if raking over an area with a comb.
Police combed the field for evidence after the assault.
La police a passé le terrain au peigne fin à la recherche de preuves après l’agression.
To turn a vessel parallel to (the track of) (a torpedo) so as to reduce one's size as a target.
Sixteen torpedo bombers divided their attention between the two ships. Repulse combed the torpedo wakes and knocked down two of the attackers.
2013, Steve Backer, British Battlecruisers of the Second World War,…
Seize bombardiers-torpilleurs se sont partagé leur attention entre les deux navires. Repulse a repéré les sillages des torpilles et abattu deux des assaillants.
To straighten one's hair with a comb. (This entry is a translation hub.)
A battle, a fight (often one in which weapons are used).
Conditions were horrendous aboard most British naval vessels at the time. Scurvy and other diseases ran rampant, killing more seamen each year than all other causes combined, including combat.
2012 March 26, William E. Carter, Merri Sue Carter, “The British…

(intransitive) To fight (with); to struggle for victory (against).
It has proven very difficult to combat drug addiction.
Il s’est révélé très difficile de lutter contre la toxicomanie.
A person engaged in combat, often armed.
Gladiators were combatants who fought to the death to entertain the public.
Les gladiateurs étaient des combattants qui se battaient à mort pour divertir le public.
The act of combining, the state of being combined or the result of combining.
She took a dangerous combination of alcohol and heroin.
Elle a pris un dangereux mélange d’alcool et d’héroïne.
The chef experimented with new flavor combinations.
Le chef a expérimenté de nouvelles associations de saveurs.
A sequence of numbers or letters used to open a combination lock.
The combination to their safe was the date of birth of their first child.
La combinaison de leur coffre-fort était la date de naissance de leur premier enfant.
(mathematics) One or more elements selected from a set without regard to the order of selection.
How many combinations of 3 cards can you draw from a deck?
Combien de combinaisons de 3 cartes peut-on tirer d’un jeu ?
An association or alliance of people for some common purpose.
(transitive) To bring (two or more things or activities) together; to unite.
I'm combining business and pleasure on this trip.
Je joins l’utile à l’agréable pendant ce voyage.
To have two or more things or properties that function together.
Joe combines the intelligence of a rock with the honesty of a politician.
Joe allie l’intelligence d’un caillou à l’honnêteté d’un politicien.
deux substances qui se combinent facilement
Resulting from the addition of several sources, parts, elements, aspects, etc. united together.
The combined efforts of the emergency workers kept the river from going over its banks, barely.
Les efforts conjugués des secouristes ont empêché, de justesse, le fleuve de sortir de son lit.
(chemistry) The act or process of burning.
(intransitive) To move nearer to the point of perspective.
She’ll be coming round the mountain when she comes the wrong way […]
Elle contournera la montagne quand elle viendra par le mauvais côté […]
Cyclists should have a red reflector on the back of their bike.
Les cyclistes doivent avoir un catadioptre rouge à l’arrière de leur vélo.
(intransitive, often vulgar, slang) To achieve orgasm; to cum; to ejaculate.
To pretend to be; to behave in the manner of; to assume the role of.
Don’t come the innocent with me — I saw you take it.
Ne joue pas les innocents avec moi : je t’ai vu le prendre.
I called the dog, but she wouldn't come.
J’ai appelé la chienne, mais elle n’a pas voulu venir.
(copulative, fossil word) To become, to turn out to be.
Don’t worry — everything will come right in the end.
Ne t’inquiète pas, tout finira par s’arranger.
To fall headlong from a horse.

e: Computer-generated graphics have come a long way in the past few decades.
Les images de synthèse ont fait d’énormes progrès au cours des dernières décennies.
(intransitive) To come to pass; to develop; to occur; to take place; to happen; to exist.
We have to ask, how did this come about?
Nous devons nous demander comment on en est arrivé là.
“Ready to come about!” shouted the skipper.
« Paré à virer ! » cria le skipper.
(idiomatic) To give an appearance or impression; to project a certain image; to seem or appear (to be some way). [(often) with as; or (often) with…
How did she come across when you met with her?
Quelle impression t’a-t-elle faite quand tu l’as rencontrée ?
(idiomatic, transitive) To find, usually by accident.
In the dark he came across an old box by accident.
Dans le noir, il tomba par hasard sur une vieille boîte.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see come, across.
He came across the street towards me.
Il traversa la rue pour venir vers moi.
To change sides; to cross over to work for the opposition.
You argued well in court but your firm doesn't pay its lawyers well, so why don't you come across to ours?
Vous avez bien plaidé, mais votre cabinet paie mal ses avocats : pourquoi ne pas passer chez nous ?
To pursue or follow; to pursue with hostile intent.
Don't try to come after me.
To follow or succeed; to be the successor of.
Who came after Richard the Lionheart?
Qui a succédé à Richard Cœur de Lion ?
(idiomatic, informal, by ellipsis) A polite formula used when one has not heard or understood what has been said, or to indicate surprise.
"Who says he did?" / "Aubry." / "Yeah? A guy in for murder? Come again." / "Glad to. Beebe says so too."
1955, Rex Stout, "When a Man Murders...", in Three Witnesses, October…
« Qui dit qu’il l’a fait ? » / « Aubry. » / « Ah ouais ? Un type en taule pour meurtre ? Tu peux répéter ? » / « Volontiers. Beebe le dit aussi. »
(idiomatic) Used as a polite farewell to a visitor, inviting a return visit.
I'd like you to come along with me to the opera.
J’aimerais que tu m’accompagnes à l’opéra.
(idiomatic, intransitive) To progress; to make progress; to quicken.
The renovation is coming along nicely, and should be ready within a month.
La rénovation avance bien et devrait être terminée d’ici un mois.
To arise, appear (make an appearance), come into being.
When the telephone first came along, it was mostly just for businesses and rich people, but eventually almost everyone got one.
Quand le téléphone est apparu, il était surtout réservé aux entreprises et aux riches, mais presque tout le monde a fini par en avoir un.
To alternately enter and exit, arrive and depart (either physically or figuratively).
He comes and goes as he pleases.
Il va et vient comme bon lui semble.
To repeatedly appear and disappear; to be transient.
My headaches come and go, but the pain in my neck is constant.
Mes maux de tête vont et viennent, mais la douleur dans ma nuque est constante.
to elapse, pass by; to occur
An eighth European final came and went for Benfica, leaving one of the world's most storied clubs still without a continental title since their twin European Cup triumphs in 1961 and 1962.
2014 May 14, Mark Lomas, “Three Things: Sevilla vs. Benfica”, in ESPN
Une huitième finale européenne est passée pour Benfica, laissant l’un des clubs les plus prestigieux du monde toujours sans titre continental depuis ses deux Coupes d’Europe de 1961 et 1962.
My old clothes are all coming apart.
Mes vieux vêtements partent tous en lambeaux.
(intransitive) To have an emotional breakdown; to become emotionally dysfunctional; to have an intense emotional reaction.
To change one's mind, especially to begin to agree or appreciate what one was reluctant to accept at first.
Give her time, and she may come around and see things your way.
Laisse-lui du temps, elle finira peut-être par changer d’avis et se ranger à ton point de vue.
To attack (someone); to harass (someone); to challenge(someone) to a fight.
As I backed away, he came at me with a knife.
Alors que je reculais, il s’est jeté sur moi avec un couteau.
To get to, especially with effort or difficulty.
His precise meaning was not easy to come at.
Le sens précis de ses propos n’était pas facile à saisir.
To accept (a situation); to agree to do; to try.
Nah, mate – I'm not going to come at that again. Too risky.
Non, mon pote, je ne vais pas retenter le coup. Trop risqué.
To return to one's possession, especially of memories.
Suddenly it all came back to him, the tea, the petite madeleines, his mother.
Soudain, tout lui revint : le thé, les petites madeleines, sa mère.
To be revived after dying; to be resurrected.
(transitive) To affect negatively or cause discord between (someone) and another person.
Our love is so strong that nothing can come between us.
Notre amour est si fort que rien ne peut se mettre entre nous.
A command to a sheepdog to move clockwise around the sheep.
When the sub got stuck, the brass kept the fact under wraps for 32 hours before Russia came clean and asked for foreign help.
2005 August 8, “Quotes of the Day”, in Time, retrieved 12 Sep 2013
Quand le sous-marin s’est retrouvé coincé, l’état-major a gardé le secret pendant 32 heures avant que la Russie ne passe aux aveux et ne demande l’aide de l’étranger.
After a clap of thunder, down came the rain.
Après un coup de tonnerre, la pluie s’abattit.
Real estate prices have come down since the peak of the boom.
Les prix de l’immobilier ont baissé depuis le pic de la flambée.
(intransitive) To reach or release a decision.
The decision in Doe v. Smith came down this morning.
La décision dans l’affaire Doe c. Smith est tombée ce matin.
Much wisdom has come down in the form of proverbs.
Beaucoup de sagesse nous a été transmise sous forme de proverbes.

L’incendie a causé de tels dégâts que tout le bâtiment devra être démoli.

Come down to my place someday and have lunch.
Passe chez moi un de ces jours, on déjeunera ensemble.

Il m’arrive tellement de bonnes choses, et je suis un homme si heureux. Je voulais écrire plus tôt, mais je n’arrivais pas à redescendre sur terre assez longtemps.
To survive to the present day; to be extant in some form.
There is some confusion about this work since the original has disappeared, and scholars have assumed that what has come down to us is not by Mozart.
2002, Alexander J. Morin, editor, Classical Music: The Listener's…
Il règne une certaine confusion sur cette œuvre, car l’original a disparu, et les spécialistes ont supposé que ce qui nous est parvenu n’est pas de Mozart.
To develop symptoms or signs of (an illness).

Avec ce mal de gorge et cette toux, j’ai l’impression de couver un rhume.
To contract or get (an illness); to show symptoms of.

So I diddled around, then came down with the money, and we were finally ready to roll.
2011, Charley Rosen, The Wizard of Odds
Alors j’ai traîné un peu, puis j’ai sorti l’argent, et nous étions enfin prêts à partir.
(idiomatic) To win first place in a competition.

Sally est arrivée première au concours de calligraphie.
(idiomatic) To be the most important thing to consider.

2014 August 29, Ruzwana Bashir, “The untold story of how a culture of…
Je témoigne publiquement de ma propre histoire dans l’espoir d’encourager d’autres personnes à faire de même et d’aider à briser le mur de silence qui perpétue les abus.
To have as one's origin, birthplace or nationality.

La plupart des touristes à Majorque viennent d’Angleterre. Ma copine vient de Suède.

Even though I have a more progressive philosophy, I can understand where he's coming from. There was a time in my life when it was hard for me to adapt to change, myself.
Même si j’ai une philosophie plus progressiste, je comprends son point de vue. Il fut un temps où j’avais moi-même du mal à m’adapter au changement.
To be motivated by decency, kindness, or good intentions.
That gushing, glowing, 2,500-word goodbye e-mail does come from a good place. That doesn't make it a good idea.
2013 August 1, Claire Suddath, “Office Etiquette: The Farewell…
Ce long courriel d’adieu de 2 500 mots, débordant d’effusions, part d’une bonne intention. Ça n’en fait pas une bonne idée pour autant.
(idiomatic) To complete a cycle of transition, returning to where one started after gaining experience or exploring other things.
The pioneers were determined to build a community in the wilderness come hell or high water.
Les pionniers étaient résolus à bâtir une communauté en pleine nature, contre vents et marées.
(figurative) To gain widespread acceptance in a group or society, especially where there was not any before.

Longtemps à l’écart de la politique occidentale, le Portugal a été réintégré après la révolution des Œillets de 1974.
Of a spy: to return home after having gone undercover in enemy territory.
I mean … one can't be out in the cold all the time; one has to come in from the cold … do you see what I mean?
1963 September, John le Carré [pseudonym; David John Moore Cornwell],…
Je veux dire… on ne peut pas rester tout le temps à l’écart ; il faut bien finir par revenir parmi les autres… tu vois ce que je veux dire ?
To prove to be useful or helpful.
This is where what I learned in High School really came in handy.
2010, Vernon Lucas, Standing in the Shadows of Street Legends,…
C’est là que ce que j’avais appris au lycée m’a vraiment servi.
To enter a scene of conflict quickly and aggressively.
The chopper came in hot, with guns blazing.
L’hélico est arrivé sous le feu, toutes armes crachant.
(idiomatic) To form; to start to exist.

Les sociologues aimeraient étudier comment ce phénomène est apparu.

C’était au début du printemps quand mon petit garçon est venu au monde.

Une des roues du chariot s’est détachée.

Il a tenté son imitation de Chaplin, mais ça n’a pas vraiment pris.

Arrête ton char, mon pote ! Tu ne peux pas être sérieux.

Le nouveau jardin prend forme joliment.

Au détour du chemin, je suis tombé sur Julia assise au bord de la rivière.

I think he's coming on too late after my line.
Je trouve qu’il entre en scène trop tard après ma réplique.

Come on, George! You can win!
Come on! You can't possibly expect me to believe that.
Arrête ! Tu ne t’attends quand même pas à ce que je croie ça.
An expression of frustration, exasperation, or impatience; hurry up.
Come on, we don't want to miss the train!
Allez, viens, on ne veut pas rater le train !

Je vais te montrer où est l’auditorium. Viens !
An expression of defiance or as a challenge; approach; come at me.

Vas-y ! Je n’ai pas peur de toi.

Come on down! Breakfast is ready!
to visit someone's home or other location.

Passe à la maison après le boulot, on commandera des pizzas.

2014, Nick Morgan, Power Cues: The Subtle Science of Leading Groups,…

Il me draguait vraiment à la fête.

Il s’est mis à neiger à la tombée de la nuit.

La souris est sortie du trou.

La chanson est sortie à la radio en 1967.

Il a fait son coming out auprès de ses amis.

Elle a fini par avouer son athéisme à sa famille religieuse.

Voilà pourquoi il est devenu bizarre.

come over for coffee and cake
venir prendre un café et du gâteau

C’est un homme raisonnable. Je savais qu’il finirait par changer d’avis.

Tu veux venir dîner ce soir ?

Après ce coup sur la tête, il m’a fallu un moment pour reprendre connaissance.

Elle reprit connaissance grâce à des sels.

Le skipper décida de mettre en panne et d’attendre que le vent tombe.

Alors, ça fait combien ? ; l’addition s’élève à 10 £ chacun
